questions.question: Compare Java's garbage collectors: G1GC, ZGC, Shenandoah, and ParallelGC.
questions.title: JVM Garbage Collectors Compared — G1, ZGC, Shenandoah, Parallel
questions.direct_answer: G1GC (default Java 9+) balances throughput and latency with <200ms target pauses. ZGC (Java 15+) achieves sub-millisecond pauses for heap-independent workloads. Parallel GC maximizes throughput with longer pauses. Choose based on latency requirements.

sections.title: Every Collector Makes a Different Bet on the Throughput-vs-Latency Spectrum
sections.content:
Choosing a garbage collector is not about finding the "best" one — it is about matching the collector's design trade-off to your workload's requirements. **Parallel GC** bets everything on throughput by stopping all application threads for collection, accepting multi-second pauses. **G1GC** aims for a middle ground, dividing the heap into regions and collecting the most garbage-dense regions first to meet a configurable pause-time target. **ZGC** and **Shenandoah** push pause times below one millisecond by performing nearly all GC work concurrently with application threads, at the cost of higher CPU overhead.

The trap is assuming newer always means better. ZGC achieves remarkable pause times, but it uses more CPU for its concurrent work and more memory for its colored pointer metadata. For a batch processing job that cares only about total execution time, Parallel GC outperforms every concurrent collector. For a Spring Boot web service with moderate latency requirements, G1GC (the default since Java 9) handles the job with minimal tuning.

**CMS** (Concurrent Mark Sweep) held the low-pause role before G1 but was removed in Java 14 due to fragmentation issues and maintenance burden. Any production system still referencing CMS should migrate to G1 or ZGC.

sections.title: Head-to-Head: Pause Time, Throughput, and When to Switch
sections.content:
The following comparison captures the essential selection criteria. The right choice depends on your latency SLA, heap size, and whether you can afford the CPU overhead of concurrent collection.

| Collector | Pause Time | Throughput | Default In | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parallel GC | Seconds (multi-thread STW) | Highest | Java 8 | Batch jobs, offline processing |
| G1GC | 100-200ms target | High | Java 9+ | General web services, 4GB+ heaps |
| ZGC | Sub-millisecond | High (more CPU) | — | Latency-critical APIs, large heaps |
| Shenandoah | Sub-millisecond | Moderate | — | Low-pause alternative (Red Hat JDK) |

**G1GC** works by dividing the heap into equal-sized regions (1-32MB) and tracking how much live data each region contains. During a pause, it evacuates the regions with the most garbage first — hence "Garbage-First." The `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` flag sets a soft target that G1 tries to meet by adjusting how many regions it collects per cycle. This region-based approach also eliminates the fragmentation problems that plagued CMS.

**ZGC** uses colored pointers and load barriers to relocate objects concurrently. Application threads see a consistent heap view because every pointer load passes through a barrier that updates references transparently. The trade-off is roughly 5-15% additional CPU overhead and approximately 3% memory overhead for the pointer metadata. For heaps under 4GB where pause times are already short with G1, the CPU cost of ZGC provides no net benefit.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Parallel GC** — highest throughput; stop-the-world pauses can last seconds; for batch processing only.
- **G1GC (default Java 9+)** — region-based; soft pause-time target via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`; good for web services.
- **ZGC** — sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size; higher CPU usage for concurrent collection work.
- **Shenandoah** — similar goals to ZGC; different algorithm; available in OpenJDK.
- **ZGC is not universally better** — on small heaps under 4GB, G1 pauses are already short; ZGC's CPU overhead provides no benefit.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java ships with four main garbage collectors, each making a different trade-off between throughput, pause duration, and CPU overhead. There is no universally best choice — the right GC algorithm depends on what your application can tolerate: long pauses for high throughput, or short pauses at higher CPU cost.

**Parallel GC:**
- Highest throughput — throws all threads at collection during stop-the-world pauses
- Pauses can last seconds — suitable for batch processing and offline analytics, not for user-facing services

**G1GC (default since Java 9):**
- Region-based heap — collects regions with the highest garbage ratio first
- Soft pause-time target via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`; adjusts collection scope to meet it
- Avoids fragmentation issues that killed CMS; good default for most web services

**ZGC:**
- Almost all work done concurrently with application threads — sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size
- Higher CPU usage for concurrent GC work
- Use when even 200ms pauses are unacceptable: algorithmic trading, real-time pricing, strict p99 SLAs

**Common mistake:**
- Assuming ZGC is universally better — on small heaps under 4GB, G1 pauses are already short; ZGC's CPU overhead provides no net benefit

I recommend G1 as the default, enabling GC logging, and only switching if p99 latency analysis shows GC pauses as the dominant contributor.

questions.question: How do you tune GC and analyze GC logs in production?
questions.title: GC Tuning and GC Log Analysis
questions.direct_answer: Enable GC logging with -Xlog:gc* and analyze with GCEasy or JVM Mission Control. Key metrics: pause frequency, pause duration, allocation rate, and promotion failure. Tune heap sizing, generation ratios, and target pause time based on findings.

sections.title: Always Collect GC Logs Before Changing Any Flags
sections.content:
The most common mistake in GC tuning is changing JVM flags based on theory instead of data. Before adjusting heap sizes, generation ratios, or pause targets, you need to know what is actually happening — how often pauses occur, how long they last, how much memory each cycle reclaims, and whether the live data set is growing over time.

**GC logging** is the foundation of any tuning effort. Java 9+ unifies logging under `-Xlog:gc*`, which captures every collection event with timestamps, heap transitions, and pause durations. Java 8 uses the older `-XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps` flags. These logs cost virtually nothing at runtime and should be enabled in every production deployment.

The critical diagnostic distinction is between **minor GC** (young generation collection), **major GC** (old generation collection), and **full GC** (entire heap compaction). Minor GCs are expected — they run frequently and complete in milliseconds. Full GCs are the problem events. They stop all application threads and can take seconds on large heaps.

Common full GC triggers include promotion failure (old generation too full to accept surviving young objects), explicit `System.gc()` calls from monitoring agents, and **Metaspace exhaustion** when dynamic class loading runs unchecked. Understanding GC logs lets you distinguish between a heap that is merely undersized (stable live set but too-frequent GC) and a genuine **memory leak** (live set growing after each full GC).

sections.title: Enable Logging, Read the Output, and Identify the Pause Pattern
sections.content:
The diagnostic workflow starts with enabling GC logging using the unified logging framework available in Java 9 and later.

```bash
java \
  -Xmx4g -Xms4g \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/ \
  -jar app.jar
```

Each GC event produces a structured log line showing the collection type, heap before and after, and pause duration. A normal young GC entry looks like `GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) 512M->480M(4096M) 8.2ms` — the 8ms pause is healthy. A full GC entry like `GC(43) Pause Full (Ergonomics) 3800M->1200M(4096M) 1850ms` signals a problem worth investigating.

Upload the log file to **GCEasy** (web-based analyzer) or open it in **GraalVM Mission Control** for visual correlation of pause times, allocation rates, and heap occupancy trends. Look for three patterns: **steadily increasing live set after full GC** (memory leak), **frequent promotion failures** (old generation undersized relative to the allocation rate), and **explicit GC events** triggered by `System.gc()` calls from libraries or monitoring agents. For the last case, adding `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC` prevents external code from forcing stop-the-world pauses.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Always start with GC logging** — `-Xlog:gc*` on Java 9+; negligible overhead; without telemetry you're guessing.
- **Distinguish minor GC from full GC** — minor is normal (10-50ms); full GC stops all threads and causes p99 latency spikes.
- **Post-GC live set stable but heap fills quickly** — heap undersized; increase `-Xmx`.
- **Post-GC live set grows steadily** — memory leak; capture heap dump with Eclipse MAT.
- **Always pair with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`** — when OOM strikes, you need the snapshot immediately.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
GC tuning in Java follows a strict discipline: measure first, diagnose second, change one flag at a time. Without baseline telemetry from GC logs, you're guessing — and changing heap sizes or GC algorithms without data typically makes things worse, not better.

**Step 1 — Enable GC logging:**
- `-Xlog:gc*` on Java 9+ — negligible overhead; provides all the telemetry needed for tuning decisions

**Step 2 — Distinguish minor GC from full GC:**
- Minor GC: reclaims young generation; typically 10-50ms; normal and expected
- Full GC: stops all application threads; can take seconds on large heaps; causes p99 latency spikes visible to users

**Diagnosing frequent full GC:**
- Post-GC live set stable but heap fills quickly → heap undersized; increase `-Xmx`
- Live set grows steadily over hours → memory leak; capture heap dump for analysis
- Sporadic full GC with no heap pressure → explicit `System.gc()` from monitoring agent or RMI; add `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`

I recommend always pairing GC logging with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` — when OOM strikes, you need the snapshot immediately rather than scrambling to reproduce after a restart.
